This page goes with **Chapter 5, Intervals** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Intervals.html).

**You already know this.** Every tonal pattern you sing is made of intervals: do–mi, mi–so, so–do. An **interval** is the distance
between two of those pitches. This chapter gives each distance a name.

**A caution from Gordon.** He argues that intervals should be learned *in a tonality and keyality*, not as bare distances: patterns
of three to five pitches carry meaning, while an interval is only two, and C up to F sounds different in F than in C (Gordon 65).
So on this page every interval starts as a pair of syllables inside a pattern you know.

Press ▶ to hear an example, or **▶ Sing** to hear it sung on syllables. Click any heading to fold its section.

## What you know → what the book calls it

| You sing | The book says |
|---|---|
| do–re, re–mi | major 2nd (M2), a whole step |
| mi–fa, ti–do | minor 2nd (m2), a half step |
| do–mi, fa–la, so–ti | major 3rd (M3) |
| re–fa, mi–so, la–do | minor 3rd (m3) |
| do–fa, so–do | perfect 4th (P4) |
| do–so, re–la, la–mi | perfect 5th (P5) |
| fa–ti (up) | augmented 4th (A4), the tritone |
| ti–fa (up) | diminished 5th (d5), the tritone |
| do–do | perfect octave (P8) |

## 5.1 Number: count the letters

[Read 5.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/IntervalsIntroduction.html)

The **number** of an interval counts letters, including both ends: C to E is C D E, a **3rd**. In syllables, count the same way:
do re mi is a 3rd. The number doesn't care about sharps or flats: C to E♭ and C to E♯ are both 3rds.

**Melodic** intervals are one note after the other (as you sing them); **harmonic** intervals sound together.

## 5.2 Quality: major, minor, perfect

[Read 5.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/HowToIdentifyIntervals.html)

The book's method measures from the lower note, as if it were **do** of a major scale:

- If the top note is in that major scale, the interval is **major** (2nds, 3rds, 6ths, 7ths) or **perfect** (unisons, 4ths, 5ths,
  octaves).
- If the top note is a half step lower than that, a major interval becomes **minor**.

You already have this: think the lower note as do, sing up to the top note, and ask whether you passed through the major scale's
notes. Up from do, every interval is major or perfect:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="80"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Up from do: M2, M3, P4, P5, M6, M7, P8
M:2/4
L:1/4
K:C
C D | C E | C F | C G | C A | C B | C c |]
w:do re do mi do fa do so do la do ti do do
</script></div>

The minor intervals come from inside your patterns. These are the ones you sing most:

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="80"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Minor intervals in patterns you know: m2, m3, m3, m6, m7
M:2/4
L:1/4
K:C
E F | D F | A, C | E c | D c |]
w:mi fa re fa la do mi do re do
</script></div>

**Counting half steps** also works and is a good check: m2 = 1, M2 = 2, m3 = 3, M3 = 4, P4 = 5, A4/d5 = 6, P5 = 7, m6 = 8, M6 = 9,
m7 = 10, M7 = 11, P8 = 12.

### Practise: name the interval

Start with the intervals up from do, then add the minor ones under **Settings**. Set **Show** to *Sound only* for ear training.

<div class="drill" data-ex="interval" data-settings="ints=M2,M3,P4,P5,M6,M7,P8&clef=treble&start=natural&dir=up&shape=melodic"></div>

## 5.3 Writing intervals

[Read 5.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/HowToWriteIntervals.html)

To write "a M6 above F": make F do, sing up to la (do re mi fa so la), and write the letter: F G A B♭ C **D**. For a minor interval,
write the major one and lower the top note a half step: a m6 above F is D♭.

## 5.4 Inversion

[Read 5.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/InversionOfIntervals.html)

Flip an interval by moving the bottom note up an octave. You already sing both halves: do up to mi is a M3, and mi up to do is a
m6. The rules:

- The numbers add to **9**: a 3rd inverts to a 6th, a 2nd to a 7th, a 4th to a 5th.
- **Major ↔ minor**, **perfect stays perfect**, **augmented ↔ diminished**.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="80"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Do–mi (M3), then mi–do (m6); do–so (P5), then so–do (P4)
M:2/4
L:1/4
K:C
C E | E c | C G | G c |]
w:do mi mi do do so so do
</script></div>

## 5.5 Augmented and diminished

[Read 5.5](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/AugmentedAndDiminishedIntervals.html)

Make a major or perfect interval a half step **larger** and it is **augmented**. Make a minor or perfect interval a half step
**smaller** and it is **diminished**. The one you already sing every day is between **fa and ti**: fa up to ti is an augmented 4th
(three whole steps, the **tritone**), and ti up to fa is a diminished 5th. Both are 6 half steps. You hear it in the dominant
seventh, so–ti–re–fa.

<div class="abc-ex" data-bpm="80"><script type="text/plain">
X:1
T:Fa up to ti (A4), ti up to fa (d5), then so–ti–re–fa
M:4/4
L:1/4
K:C
F B B f | G B d f |]
w:fa ti ti fa so ti re fa
</script></div>

## Bridging: from syllable pairs to names

1. **Hear it in a pattern.** Find the two pitches inside a tonal pattern you know.
2. **Name the syllables.** "Re up to fa."
3. **Count the letters** for the number: re mi fa = 3rd.
4. **Check the quality** against do: from re, the major 3rd would be fa♯ (re is do of D major: D E F♯). Fa is a half step lower:
   **minor 3rd**.
5. **Check by half steps** if you're unsure.

## Check yourself

1. Name the interval do up to la.
2. Name the interval la up to do.
3. Mi up to ti: number and quality?
4. Invert a M2. What do you get?
5. Write a m3 above G.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers
1. Major 6th.
2. Minor 3rd (it's the inversion of do–la).
3. Perfect 5th (mi fa so la ti, 7 half steps).
4. A minor 7th.
5. B♭ (major 3rd G–B, lowered a half step).
:::

All the interval drills are on [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd?ex=interval). Next: [Triads](triads.qmd).
